You plant your foot on the crumbling edge to throw yourself across the drop, but your sole finds only black ice. Your weight twists. Instead of sailing clear across the chasm to the far stone, your body collides hard with the sheer rock face yards below the rim. The stone hammers into your ribs and hip with a dull crunch. You slide, fingers tearing against frozen moss and flint, before your boots wedge into a narrow shelf above the drop. Pain flares where the blow landed, and when you haul yourself upright against the frozen rock wall, your left knee buckles; you stagger, leaning hard against the cliff to keep from tipping into the void, favoring one leg.

The hound-barks you were running from are gone. There is only the low rush of water down in the gorge and the rattle of pebbles falling from where you struck. Above you, where the hounds should have burst onto the ledge, an iron-shod staff strikes the rim instead. The Hound-Master peers down over the break of stone, but the dogs are nowhere behind him—only a hooded woman wrapped in soiled sheepskins, standing at his shoulder with an unstrung yew bow in her calloused hands. She was not with him at the crossing. 

The Hound-Master spits over the edge, the glob of phlegm dropping into the mist below. “Climb up or drop, scribe,” he says, his voice flat as wet slate. He plants his boot on a loose boulder directly above your narrow foothold and leans his weight onto the stone.

verdicts.weakness: Kael hauling himself upright adds an action the player did not choose.

The leap carries you outward over the drop, the wind roaring up from the cold river below, but the launch lacks purchase. You strike the opposing lip hard, chest and ribs slamming against bare granite. Your fingers scrabble for seams in the frozen stone, tearing through damp wool and skin, but the sheer rock offers no grip. Gravity pulls you backward and down, dropping you onto a narrow spur of jagged shale five feet below the rim with a jarring, bone-deep impact. Pain flares where the blow landed against your hip and knee. You stagger upright, breath sawing through locked teeth, your weight forcing you to favor one leg as the joint grinds in its socket. 

The baying of the hounds is gone. The silence that replaces the pack is thick, broken only by the steady drip of thaw-water and the drone of the dusk wind through the cleft. Above you, boots grind on the upper shelf. The Hound-Master leans over the break, but the leashes in his gloved fist hang empty, the leather straps severed clean by an axe-stroke. Beside him stands a woman clad in scorched iron plate, a broad-bladed spear resting across her shoulder—no hunter of the local lord, but an inquisitor of the Sunken Spire. She does not look down at the gorge, her gaze fixed entirely on the high path behind you.

The Hound-Master spits over the edge, the dark knot of tobacco landing on the stone inches from your boot. He does not loose an arrow or shout an order; he simply plants his heavy frame in the only chimney of rock that climbs back to the plateau, arms folded across his salt-stained jerkin as the woman steps past him toward the southern trail. The frost on the rock face gleams dull grey against the dying light, the drop behind your heels sheer and black.

verdicts.weakness: The new inquisitor and her faction introduce unnecessary lore that distracts from the failed leap.

Her fingers are blackened with old gall-ink to the second knuckle, and the tension in her shoulders pulls her wool tunic tight across her collarbone. A drip of water strikes a lead sheet somewhere in the collapsed stacks behind her with a dull, rhythmic tap.

When you ask who the volume belongs to and what price she sets on it, her jaw tightens. She does not look down at the bound leather between your elbows. "Step back from the wood," she says, her voice level and sharp as chipped flint. "It belonged to the bailiff of the lower settlement, and you will leave it where it sits or I will open your throat with this scraper."

She holds the blade flat, the edge catching the tallow light, and sets her left palm hard against the ledger to draw it six inches closer to her side of the plank. Then she turns her face toward the dark corridor leading to the lower vaults, silent, waiting for your boots to move.

Greywater’s central well sits in the noon damp, its circular stonework wet with grease and dark moss. You stand over the pit, looking Widow Sarn dead in the face, and ask her plainly if she put something into the settlement’s water. The scent of bruised tansy and wet earth drifts from the willow basket hooked over her crooked elbow. Overhead, crows shift along the thatch eaves of a nearby hovel, shaking cold rainwater from their wings. Your knuckles stay pressed to your coat, your ribs aching beneath the wool where the bruises have set hard and tender from the road. 

Widow Sarn does not blink. The skin around her jaw pulls tight as leather stretched across a dry frame. She spits into the mud beside your boot, the fluid dark with chewed root. “Keep your tongue behind your teeth, traveler, or I’ll see your mouth sewn shut with tallow thread,” she says. “The water turned black before I ever dug these roots.” She snaps a woody stalk between her thumb and forefinger, dropping the broken stem into her basket, and turns her back on you to limp toward the low gate. 

Beyond the well, an iron pail lies dented in the gravel, left tipped on its side where someone dropped it in haste. The noon air hangs flat and cold over the muddy square, carrying the sour smoke of damp peat from the chimneyless huts. Widow Sarn’s wooden clogs strike the wet stones with a dull, hollow rhythm until she rounds the timber corner of the drying shed.

Each step drags through submerged debris—cracked flagstones, rotted timber, and loose gravel that rolls under your boots. A single tallow dip burns in an alcove fifty paces back, its pale gleam barely cutting the murk, while the far stair remains swallowed in blackness. Halfway across the chamber, your foot wedges into a sunken gap between the stones. A sharp crack snaps through the deep water, followed by a heavy impact against your shin as a displaced slab shifts beneath your weight. Pain flares where the blow landed. He looks down at your struggle in the mire, spatters a mouthful of bitter root into the black pool near your chest, and wedges the iron bar behind the heavy oak hoist above, letting loose the counterweight.
